article.title: Designing Metrics for Agentic AI: Measuring Outcomes, Control, and Recovery
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Agentic AI systems can plan, call tools, modify external state, and continue through multiple steps. Traditional model metrics such as answer accuracy remain useful, but they are not sufficient for evaluating a system that takes actions. The measurement framework must include outcomes, control, efficiency, and recovery. Task success is the starting point. Did the system actually complete the user's goal under the stated constraints? Success should be defined at the workflow level rather than by whether individual model responses looked reasonable. A travel agent that finds good flights but books the wrong date has failed the task. Constraint adherence is a separate dimension. The agent may reach the goal while violating a budget, permission rule, data-handling requirement, or user preference. These failures can be rare but costly, so they should not disappear inside an average success score. Tool-call quality matters because agentic systems depend on external actions. Metrics can track invalid calls, unnecessary calls, failed calls, retries, and the share of actions that require correction. However, fewer calls are not automatically better. An additional verification call can be valuable when the cost of an incorrect action is high. State accuracy is also important. Long workflows require the agent to maintain facts, intermediate results, and commitments. Losing track of which file was updated or which customer was selected can create cascading errors. Tests should therefore include multi-step state consistency. Human intervention rate is useful but must be interpreted carefully. A lower rate can indicate better autonomy, or it can indicate that the system is failing silently instead of escalating. Intervention should be evaluated together with error severity and escalation quality. Recovery is a core capability. Real tools time out, APIs return partial results, permissions change, and users revise requirements. Measure whether the agent detects failure, preserves completed work, chooses a safe retry strategy, and resumes without duplicating irreversible actions. Idempotency is especially important for payments, messages, file writes, and bookings. A retry should not accidentally execute the same side effect twice. Cost and latency belong in the framework because long autonomous loops can consume significant resources. Track model tokens, tool costs, wall-clock time, and steps per successful task. The useful denominator is often cost per successful, policy-compliant completion rather than cost per model call. Observability supports all of these metrics. Logs should connect user intent, plan, tool calls, tool results, state transitions, approvals, and final outcomes. Without traceability, aggregate scores are difficult to diagnose. Evaluation sets should include normal tasks, ambiguous requests, tool failures, conflicting constraints, and adversarial or unusual inputs. Production monitoring should then compare real traffic with these tested conditions. Outcome quality can also be delayed. An agent may complete a workflow successfully but create downstream rework or customer dissatisfaction. Follow-up metrics can capture reversals, corrections, complaints, and human cleanup. Governance metrics should track actions that require approval, policy exceptions, access violations, and whether sensitive operations used the correct authorization path. These measures make control visible rather than assuming that successful completion implies safe operation. A mature scorecard therefore combines task success, constraint adherence, tool reliability, state consistency, escalation, recovery, idempotency, cost, latency, and downstream quality. The objective is not maximum autonomy. It is dependable autonomy: the system should complete useful work, stay inside boundaries, recognize when it is uncertain, and recover safely when the environment does not behave as expected.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it. paragraphs.ja: 日本語解説：Agentic AIはtask successだけでなくcontrol、recovery、idempotency、cost、downstream qualityをworkflow単位で評価する。
